summary: Defines a metric for variation in packet delay across Internet paths, based on differences in the one-way delay of selected packets. It works when the two measuring hosts have synchronized clocks and when they do not.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how to measure the way packet travel times vary along a path. The trick is that it compares the delay of one packet with the delay of another, so the two hosts do not need perfectly synchronized clocks for the answer to be useful.

questions: what is ip packet delay variation
what is the ippm delay variation metric
does delay variation need synchronized clocks
subtitle: A precise way to measure how much packet travel times wobble, without needing perfectly synchronized clocks.

tldr.problem: People talk about network "jitter" but mean different things by it, and measuring delay between two hosts normally needs tightly synchronized clocks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines IP packet delay variation (ipdv) as the difference between the one-way delays of two selected packets, and builds a singleton, a sample and several statistics on top of it.
tldr.outcome: Because it is a difference of two delays, clock errors largely cancel out, so the metric works with synchronized and unsynchronized clocks. It sets no good or bad thresholds.

facts.label: Metric unit
facts.value: Real number of seconds (positive, zero or negative) or undefined

facts.label: Minimum packets
facts.value: At least two in the stream

today: RFC 3393 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets no required values for delay variation; it only defines how to measure and report it, and it builds on RFC 2679 and RFC 2330.

sections.title: What Delay Variation Is and Why Measure It
sections.content:
This memo defines a metric for the variation in delay of packets that flow from one host to another through an IP path. It is based on the one-way delay metric for IPPM in RFC 2679, and part of the text is taken directly from that document.

One important use of delay variation is sizing the play-out buffers of applications that need regular delivery of packets, such as voice or video, where what matters is the maximum delay variation. Other uses include working out the dynamics of the queues inside a network or a router, by linking changes in delay variation to changes in the queue length process on a link or a combination of links.

The metric is also particularly robust with respect to differences and variations in the clocks of the two hosts, so it can be used even when the hosts running the measurement points are not synchronized. In that case the measurement can also give an indication of the reciprocal skew of the clocks, and corrections are possible. The precision is often comparable with what synchronized clocks give, being of the same order of magnitude as the synchronization errors.

The goal is a metric that can be parameterized for various purposes, and any report of the metric must include all its parameters so that the conditions and the meaning of the metric are determined exactly. Since the metric expresses no value judgement, that is, it does not define what is good and what is bad, the RFC deliberately sets no particular values that IP networks must meet.
sections.plainLanguage: Delay variation matters most when you size a buffer for live audio or video, and when you want to see how queues inside the network are filling and emptying. Measuring it as a difference between two packets makes it far less sensitive to clock errors.

sections.title: Why the RFC Avoids the Word Jitter
sections.content:
The variation in packet delay is sometimes called jitter, but the RFC says that the term causes confusion because different groups use it in different ways.

The first common meaning is the variation of a signal with respect to some clock signal, where the arrival of the signal is expected to coincide with the arrival of the clock signal. This meaning is used for synchronous signals and might be used to measure the quality of circuit emulation, for example. There is also a metric called wander used in this context.

The second meaning has to do with the variation of a metric, such as delay, with respect to some reference metric, such as the average delay or the minimum delay. This meaning is frequently used by computer scientists and frequently, but not always, refers to variation in delay.

The RFC therefore avoids the word jitter wherever possible and sticks to delay variation, which it calls more precise.
sections.plainLanguage: Jitter can mean the wobble of a signal against a clock, or the wobble of one delay measurement against another. The RFC uses the longer name to avoid the argument.

sections.title: The Singleton Metric: Type-P-One-way-ipdv
sections.content:
The singleton metric defines a single instance of a delay variation measurement. On its own it is only statistically significant when combined with other instances, and it is not meant to be meaningful by itself.

The delay variation of a pair of packets within a stream of packets is defined for a selected pair going from measurement point MP1 to measurement point MP2, and it is the difference between the one-way delays of the two selected packets. The first Type P packet to pass MP1 after I1 is given index 0 and the last to pass before I2 the highest index. The metric is the difference between the value of the type-P one-way delay at T2 and its value at T1, where T1 is the wire-time at which the source sent the first bit of the first packet and T2 the wire-time at which it sent the first bit of the second.

The value is either a real number of seconds, which may be positive, zero or negative, or an undefined number of seconds. It is undefined when the source sent the two packets but the destination did not receive one or both of them.

There must be a stream of at least two packets for a singleton measurement to take place, and the selection function says exactly which two packets of the stream are used. Examples of a selection function are consecutive Type-P packets in the interval, packets with specified indices, the packets with the minimum and maximum one-way delays, and the packets with specified indices from the set of all packets with a defined delay. The packets of the stream must all be the same length, because delay depends on packet size, and the packet size is therefore a parameter of the measurement that must be reported with it.
sections.plainLanguage: One measurement compares two packets from the same stream. The answer is the difference between their delays, and it can be negative, zero or positive. Which two packets are compared is a choice the caller makes, and it has to be reported.

sections.title: How a Measurement Is Made
sections.content:
The methodology assumes the measurement is done in real time as part of an active measurement, though the same thing can be done afterwards, once the one-way delay measurement is complete.

After time I1, the source selects the source and destination addresses and forms test packets of the given Type-P, for example with the Poisson sampling technique. Any padding needed only to make the packet a given size should be filled with randomized bits, so that the measured delay is not lower than it would otherwise be because of compression along the path. The destination arranges to receive the packets. The source puts a time stamp in the packet and sends it, and the destination takes a time stamp as soon as possible on arrival. Subtracting the two time stamps gives an estimate of the one-way delay.

If the packet meets the criterion for the first packet of the pair, that delay value is recorded; otherwise packets keep being generated until the criterion is met or I2, whichever comes first. The same is then done for the second packet, and the difference between the two delay values is the delay variation of the pair. If one or both packets fail to arrive within a reasonable time, the delay variation is undefined.

A packet that is duplicated on the path counts as received, and the first copy to arrive sets its one-way delay. A packet that is fragmented and never reassembled is deemed lost. The stream is assumed to be generated with the Poisson sampling methodology, because that gives an unbiased and uniformly distributed sampling of the times between I1 and I2; a constant bit rate stream is also possible, but the effects of aliasing have to be avoided.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender stamps each test packet with a time, the receiver stamps it on arrival, and the difference gives the delay. Two such delays are subtracted to get the variation. Packets that never arrive make the result undefined.

sections.title: Clock Errors and Unsynchronized Clocks
sections.content:
The factors that affect the measurement are the same as for the one-way delay metric, but their influence is different. If the error affecting the first delay measurement were the same as the one affecting the second, they would cancel when the delay variation is calculated, and the residual error is the difference of the errors that change between T1 and T2. Errors in synchronization between the source and destination clocks contribute to both delay measurements.

The effect of skew and drift can be quantified. If the skew is linear in time, the error added to the difference of two time stamps is K times the time between them, where K is a constant. If drift cannot be ignored and is itself linear, the skew is a quadratic function of time and the error added is a linear term plus a squared term in the time between the stamps. The RFC claims that the effect of skew is small over the time scales in question, since temperature variations in a system are slow relative to packet inter-transmission times and the range of drift is so small. The maximum range of drift for commercial crystals is about 50 parts per million, and it is mainly connected with variations in operating temperature from 0 to 70 degrees Celsius.

The difference between host time and wire time decomposes into a constant part and a variable part, and only the variable part produces measurement errors, because the constant part cancels. Where the clocks are not synchronized, the RFC shows that the skew parameter can be estimated from the mean time between packets and the sample mean delay variation, and the values can then be corrected by subtracting the estimated skew times the time between each pair. The displacement caused by the skew does not change the shape of the distribution, and the standard deviation stays the same; what distorts the distribution is the effect of the drift.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the metric subtracts two delays, most clock errors cancel out. What is left is the small amount the clocks drift between the two packets, and the RFC shows how to correct for it.

sections.title: Samples and Statistics
sections.content:
A sample is what makes it possible to compute statistics over a sequence of measurements. The singleton definition is applied to a stream of test packets generated with a pseudo-random Poisson process of average arrival rate lambda, and the interval can be divided into sub-intervals if needed. The result is a sequence of measurements that can be analysed statistically. Each element of the sample is a triple: the transmission times of the two packets, and the delay variation in seconds.

Because a pseudo-random number sequence is used, the sequence of times, and so the value of the sample, is not fully specified, and a good quality pseudo-random number generator is needed. The Poisson process is used to avoid the effects of self-synchronization and to capture a sample that is as unbiased as possible, though the RFC notes that there is no claim that real Internet traffic arrives in a Poisson process.

Several statistics are then suggested, on the understanding that they are computed from a sample of reasonable size. The purpose is not to define every possible statistic but those that have been proposed or used. Lost packets complicate the statistics, because a sample mean cannot be computed when packets are lost; one way round it is to condition on the event that the selected packet pairs arrive, which in practice means throwing out the samples where one or both packets has an undefined delay.
sections.plainLanguage: One measurement is not much use, so the RFC defines a way of collecting many of them at random times and then summarizing the results.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The one-way delay variation metric has the same security properties as the one-way delay metric, so it inherits the security considerations of that document. The RFC highlights three points.

There could still be a denial of service attack by sending many measurement packets into the network, and legitimate measurements must have their parameters chosen carefully so that they do not interfere with normal traffic. The packets contain no user information, so the privacy of user data is not a concern. And there could be attempts to disrupt the measurements by diverting or corrupting the packets, so packet authentication and integrity checks may be used to make sure the test packets are valid and were not altered in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring the network means sending traffic into it, so the parameters have to be chosen so the test does not get in the way of real traffic. The test packets carry no user data.

items.title: Clock synchronization
items.text: The source and destination clocks are not set to the same time.

items.title: Skew and drift
items.text: The clocks run at slightly different rates, and that rate changes slowly.

items.title: Wire time and host time
items.text: The time a host stamps a packet is not exactly the time the bits left the wire.

items.title: Lost packets
items.text: A packet that never arrives makes the measurement undefined.
